reasoning: This is a narrative review article synthesizing existing literature on the neurochemistry, circuits, symptoms, and treatments of cognitive impairment in schizophrenia. It does not report the generation or use of any research software (no code, tools, or computational pipelines are described as being created or applied by the authors), nor does it involve the generation or analysis of original research data (no new datasets, experiments, or empirical analyses are presented). The paper purely reviews and discusses findings from previously published studies across genetics, neuroimaging, pharmacology, and clinical trials without conducting any new data collection or software-based analysis itself.

This is a consensus clinical guideline paper that synthesizes existing literature (systematic reviews, case reports, case series, and clinical trials) on the diagnosis and management of catatonia. It does not describe the creation or use of any research software - no code, tools, or computational workflows are developed or employed in producing this guideline. Similarly, it does not generate new research data (no original dataset, patient cohort, or experiment was conducted) nor does it substantively use a specific existing research dataset for analysis - instead it reviews and synthesizes findings from many prior studies narratively to produce clinical recommendations. The cited studies' own data are not reused for new analysis here; this is a literature-based consensus/guideline document. Therefore it falls into the No Software, No Data category.

The study uses existing software (TopoToolbox V2, ArcGIS Web AppBuilder) as a utility to process the DEM, rather than creating/extending new research software. However, the paper generates a new national-scale geodatabase of catchment characteristics (91 morphometric/topographic attributes for 128 catchments) derived from the DEM, which is a substantive new research dataset enabling new knowledge about Philippine river catchments. Thus software is used (not generated) and data is generated.

The paper develops a new software tool, MGDrawVis, implementing the Jaya algorithm (first application to graph drawing) along with an enhanced version using Latin Hypercube Sampling, representing significant software creation that generates new knowledge (novel algorithm application and improvement). This software is shared via OSF. Additionally, the research generates new data by creating synthetic random graph datasets (using Erdős–Rényi model) specifically for benchmarking across multiple experimental phases (tuning, Phase I-III, scalability testing), which constitutes generated research data. While real-world datasets are also used (existing data), the paper's core contribution includes generation of both software (the visualization tool and algorithm implementation) and data (synthetic benchmark graphs), placing it in the Generated category for both axes.

This is a study protocol for a planned randomized clinical trial (ERiC trial) that has not yet reported results. It describes planned data collection (questionnaires, tasks, interviews) and planned use of existing tools (R for randomization, REDCap for data management) but these are standard utility software, not research software generated or materially used to produce new knowledge at this stage. No actual research data has been generated or analyzed yet - the paper only describes methods and procedures for future data collection. Per the criteria, protocols describing planned data/software use (not yet realized) should be classified as S3D3 unless there is clear evidence of actual use/generation of data or software in the research reported. The paper mentions using CORC historical data only for power calculation justification, which is a minor, non-substantive use rather than the research generating new knowledge from that data within this paper.

The paper is a survey-based study collecting new quantitative (Likert scale) and qualitative (interview/thematic) data from nurses and midwives on genomics competencies, confidence and importance. This constitutes newly generated research data (survey responses, thematic analysis results) that underpins the findings - thus D1. Analysis was done using standard tools like Microsoft Excel and generic statistical tests (t-test, ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis), which are utility software not created or substantively extended as part of the research, and no bespoke research software was developed or used to generate new knowledge - thus S3.

This is an editorial/special issue introduction summarizing and assessing seven accepted papers using a quality assessment scale (MQAS). It does not itself generate or use any research software or research data; it merely reviews and ranks other papers' contributions descriptively. No new software was created or used by the editors, and no new dataset was generated or analyzed by this editorial itself - it only reports on datasets/software used in the reviewed papers, not in this paper's own research process.

The study uses existing software tools (NiftyReg for registration, Varian Eclipse TPS for treatment planning) as utilities rather than developing new research software - these generate new knowledge when applied but are not created/extended by the researchers (S2). The paper generates new research data: patient-specific ADC-derived cell density maps, voxelated TCP maps, BTV definitions, and SIB dose escalation plans for 10 GBM patients - this is novel substantive data created through the research process that didn't exist before (D1), going beyond simply using existing clinical imaging data by transforming it into new biological target volumes and TCP maps.

The researchers developed an innovative multiplexed immunofluorescence digital image analysis workflow (including novel dynamic image thresholding and colocalisation-based resolution techniques) implemented in open-source software, which was custom-built/extended for this research and generated new knowledge (cell phenotyping with validated accuracy metrics) - this constitutes Software Generated (S1). They also generated substantive new research data: multispectral immunofluorescence images and derived single-cell phenotype datasets from archival NLPHL/THRLBCL/LRcHL/tonsil biopsies, analyzing hundreds of image tiles with millions of phenotyped cell detections - this is newly generated research data used to produce novel biological findings about tumor microenvironment immune cell phenotypes, classifying as Data Generated (D1).

The researchers manually coded the GMDH neural network algorithm steps in MATLAB, but this appears to be an implementation of an existing well-known algorithm (GMDH, developed in 1968 by Ivakhnenko) rather than creation of novel research software - it's used as a utility/tool to generate predictions, not generating new methodological knowledge itself. SPSS was also used as an off-the-shelf statistical tool. Thus software counts as S2 (used, not generated) since no new software artifact is being contributed as a research output. On the data side, the paper describes collecting original survey data from 384 startup managers/employees via questionnaires (BRCS, MBI-GS, and a custom COVID-19 stress questionnaire), which was gathered specifically for this research (noting it reuses data collection methodology from a previous paper, but the dataset itself was collected for this study's analysis, extending/building on prior data collection). This constitutes generation of new research data, as the survey responses are the substantive data enabling the findings. Hence D1 applies.

The paper reports new experimental research data generated specifically for this study: a novel crystal structure of Mcl-1 bound to AMG-176 (deposited to PDB as 8AV9), NMR spectroscopy data (15N-HSQC, NOE, chemical shift data) for free-ligand conformational analysis, and biophysical/biochemical measurements (SPR, FRET, cellular potency assays) summarized in Table 1. This generated data (crystal structure, NMR conformers) is central to the new knowledge produced (discovery of ligand preorganization/rigidity as a design principle), so it qualifies as Research Substantive Data Generated (D1). Regarding software, the paper uses existing computational/analysis tools (MD simulation, DFT calculation, PP/PLB scoring methods, ECHOS-NMR analysis) but does not report creating or significantly extending any new research software; these are standard existing tools used as utilities to analyze data rather than software that itself generates new knowledge as a research contribution. Thus no research software is generated, and the existing tools are used merely as routine utilities, fitting S3 (No Research Software).

This is a cluster RCT in which the researchers collected original primary data (surveys, anthropometric measurements, clinical records) from pregnant women and their children across 8 clinics over 2 years, generating a new dataset specifically for this study (substantive data generated). While statistical analyses were run using the 'blme' package in R, this is a standard existing statistical software tool used as a utility for mixed-effects modeling rather than software created or substantially extended as part of the research; it does not constitute research software generation. Thus the paper fits No Software / Data Generated.

This study uses existing secondary EHR datasets (CPRD Gold and UK Biobank linked primary care data), which are pre-existing research data sources used (not newly generated) for this analysis. The paper develops 'harmonised phenotypes' (codelists of Read v2/CTV3 codes) to identify symptoms, but these phenotypes are code lists/classification schemes applied to existing data rather than research software (no scripts/applications/executables are described as created); statistical analysis used standard tools (Poisson models) which are utility software, not a generated research software artifact. Thus no software was generated or used as a substantive research software tool - standard statistical packages are implied but not emphasized as novel research software (S3). Data was used from existing CPRD and UK Biobank sources (D2), not newly collected/generated data.

This is a perspective/opinion paper discussing decolonisation of the psychology curriculum, drawing on existing literature, historical accounts, and commentary. It does not involve the creation or use of any research software, nor does it generate or use any research data (datasets, corpora, etc.). It is purely a narrative/discursive piece synthesizing prior literature and arguments, with no empirical data collection or software tools involved.

This is a data descriptor paper presenting DOCU-CLIM, a newly compiled global dataset of 621 documentary climate time series, including data rescue of previously undigitized records (e.g., Russian river ice phenology). This clearly constitutes generation of substantive research data that enables new knowledge (climate reconstructions, forward model evaluations, volcanic eruption case study). Regarding software, the paper mentions standard statistical methods (regression, forward models) and provides simple R-code to read data files, but no new research software/tool was developed or is central to generating new knowledge - existing statistical techniques are used as routine utilities rather than as a research software contribution. Hence S3 (no significant research software) and D1 (data generated).

The study generated novel substantive research data: eDNA metabarcoding data from a dated 100-year sedimentary archive of Lake Ring, chemical fingerprinting (DDT quantification), and compiled climate/biocide records, which together form new empirical datasets central to the paper's findings (D1). For software, the paper exclusively uses existing, established tools and packages (QIIME2, DADA2, PICRUST2, ANCOM, cutadapt, FastQC, ggplot2, pheatmap, sCCA implementations) without describing the creation or significant extension of new software; these existing tools were used to analyze the generated data and produce new knowledge, qualifying as S2 (Software Used) rather than S1 or S3.

This is a narrative/state-of-the-art review article discussing various imaging techniques (PET, SPECT, MRI/DCE, ASL, CT) for assessing blood-brain barrier dysfunction across different neurological diseases. It does not report original research involving generation or use of research software, nor does it involve the generation or use of research datasets. The paper synthesizes existing literature and explains imaging principles and clinical applications, without presenting new data collection, analysis, or software tools. Thus it falls under 'No Software' and 'No Data'."

This is a cross-sectional survey study collecting primary data from 10,007 respondents in Malang, Indonesia regarding COVID-19 knowledge and vaccine uptake, which constitutes newly generated research data (D1). The analysis software used (KoboToolbox for survey administration and STATA 17.1 for statistical analysis) are existing/standard tools used as utilities for data collection and analysis rather than research software created or substantively extended by this study, so S3 applies (no new research software was generated or used to create new knowledge beyond standard statistical tooling).

This is a narrative review article synthesizing findings from previously published GWAS, post-GWAS, and functional studies on microglia in AD and PD. The authors did not generate or substantially use any specific research software themselves (they discuss tools like FUMA, MAGMA, DeepSea, CADD, sLDSC as used by cited external studies, not by the authors of this review), nor did they generate or analyze any original research data. The paper is purely a literature synthesis/discussion without new software or data artifacts produced by the authors.

This is a narrative review article summarizing and synthesizing existing literature on MAIT cells and the microbiome. It does not report generation of new research software or new research data; rather it discusses findings from numerous previously published studies (mouse models, human cohorts, in vitro experiments) without conducting new experiments, analyses, or data collection itself. No software tools are developed or substantively used by the authors, and no new datasets are generated or analyzed as part of this paper.

The paper develops a novel counterfactual GAN (adapted from Choi et al.'s StarGAN framework with significant modifications for OCT image counterfactual generation, plus referee networks for age/sex/identity prediction) - this constitutes newly generated research software that creates new knowledge (synthetic counterfactual OCT images and longitudinal time series not previously obtainable). The paper also uses existing data (UK Biobank OCT image dataset) as training/testing data for the model - this is used data, not generated, as the UK Biobank dataset was not created by this research team. Since software is generated (S1) and data is used but not generated (D2), the classification is S1D2.

The researchers generated new simulated narrative data by perturbing GPT-2's text-generation parameters (temperature and memory span), creating a novel dataset of narratives rated by clinicians - this is research data generation. They also used GPT-2 as existing software, but the Python tutorial/pipeline they built to simulate perturbations and apply various NLP metrics (combining models, computing custom semantic distance measures, tangentiality calculations) constitutes a novel computational workflow/tool created for this research purpose, which generates new knowledge about which NLP metrics best capture theoretical FTD mechanisms. This simulation framework and accompanying tutorial represents generated research software, while the simulated narrative dataset and clinical ratings represent generated research data.

This is a study protocol describing a planned future survey (PRESS survey) that has not yet been conducted - it describes methods that "will be" used, not results already obtained. No actual data has been collected or generated yet (survey distribution and analysis are planned/future), and no research software was developed (Qualtrics is used merely as a commercial survey utility tool, not research software created for this study). Per the criteria, planned/proposed artefacts and protocols without evidence of actual use/generation should be classified as S3D3.

This paper reports two phase 1 clinical trials generating new pharmacokinetic data on drug-drug interactions between rezafungin and various coadministered drugs. The data (PK parameters, concentration-time profiles, AUC, Cmax values) were newly generated through clinical experimentation, qualifying as D1 (substantive data generated). For software, the researchers used existing commercial tools (Phoenix WinNonlin for noncompartmental PK analysis and SAS for statistical analysis) as standard utility tools for analysis rather than creating or substantially extending any software. These are established commercial software packages used in a routine analytical capacity, not research software developed as part of this study, so this falls under S2 (software used) rather than S1 or S3, since the analysis was essential to deriving the PK conclusions but the tools themselves were pre-existing standard packages.

This paper describes a methodological/operationalisation study using existing UK Biobank data (anthropometric, physical activity, dietary 24h assessment and FFQ data) to calculate adherence scores to WCRF/AICR cancer prevention recommendations. No new research software was created or described - standard statistical calculations and existing classification systems (NOVA) were applied, but no software tool/package was developed as a research output. However, substantive existing data (UK Biobank cohort data) was used extensively to generate new derived scores/variables (e.g., adherence scores for 158,415 and 314,616 participants), which constitutes generating new knowledge from used data. Since the data itself (UK Biobank) was not newly collected by this study but used from an existing resource, this falls under D2 (Data Used) rather than D1. No software generation is evident, so S3 applies.

This is a narrative literature review appraising existing cardiovascular risk prediction methods, biomarkers, machine learning studies, and ocular imaging techniques reported by other researchers. It does not generate or use any software/tool as part of conducting the review itself, nor does it collect, generate, or analyse any new research dataset - it synthesises findings from previously published studies. No new software was created, no existing research software was applied by the authors to produce new results, and no new or existing dataset was analysed within this paper.

The study uses existing software (Joinpoint Regression Programme v4.6.0.0, a utility statistical analysis tool, not created by the authors) to analyze existing data (Google Trends search volume data and CDC case data), both of which are pre-existing external resources used to generate new findings. No new software or research dataset was created; the researchers downloaded existing Google Trends data and applied established joinpoint regression software to analyze it, classifying as Software Used (S2) and Data Used (D2).

This is a qualitative study using semi-structured in-depth interviews with 30 Dental Officers and 17 Dental Managers in Fiji, analyzed through manual thematic analysis (no research software was created or used for analysis - transcription was manual via Microsoft Word, a standard utility tool, not research software). The research generated new qualitative data (interview transcripts) which were coded and analyzed to produce themes - this is substantive research data generated specifically for this study. No research software was developed or employed in a way that generated new knowledge; data analysis was manual thematic coding by the investigators.

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that synthesizes data from 76 previously published studies and national surveys (DHS, national micronutrient survey) on adolescent nutrition in Ethiopia - it uses existing research data (D2) rather than generating new primary data. For software, the authors explicitly state they used STATA version 17 to perform the meta-analysis (random effects model, REML, forest plots) - this is existing statistical software used as a tool to generate new knowledge (pooled prevalence estimates), which falls under S2 (Software Used) rather than no software, since STATA was integral to producing the meta-analytic results reported in the paper. No new software was created, and no new primary research data was generated - rather existing published study data was extracted, compiled, and analyzed.

The study collected new experimental data (HD-sEMG, force recordings, motor unit decomposition data) from TD and DCD children, which constitutes newly generated research data substantive to the findings (D1). The software used (Delsys NeuroMap/EMGworks, Labchart, custom MATLAB/PsychoPy scripts) are existing commercial/utility tools and bespoke scripts used for analysis/data acquisition but not described as novel research software contributing new methodological knowledge - they are used as standard utilities/off-the-shelf decomposition algorithms, so this is S3 (no research software generated or substantively used as a novel contribution).
